questions.q: Define situational irony and give one example from "Birth" where the outcome of the night call is the opposite of what Andrew anticipated when he left with Joe Morgan.
questions.a: Situational irony occurs when the actual outcome of a situation is starkly different from what was expected. In "Birth," Andrew anticipates a routine, perhaps burdensome midwifery case ("he had no premonition that this night call would prove unusual") but it becomes the defining moment of his career where he saves both mother and child, making him feel he has "done something real at last." A wrong answer (e.g., confusing it with dramatic irony or citing the chloroform conversation) reveals the student cannot distinguish between types of irony or locate the central situational reversal in the plot.

questions.q: Explain in your own words how the "alternating hot and cold water" treatment functions as a symbol in the story. What abstract idea does this physical action represent?
questions.a: The alternating hot and cold water symbolizes the desperate, rhythmic struggle between life and death — a physical enactment of the doctor's battle to pull the child back from the brink. It represents the seesaw of hope and despair, the thin margin separating existence from non-existence. A wrong answer (e.g., "it's just a medical procedure" or "it symbolizes Andrew's confusion") shows the student reads only literally and cannot extrapolate a concrete action to its thematic significance.

questions.q: Identify the type of irony present when the old grandmother says, "Susan said not to give her the chloroform if it would harm the baby. She's awful set upon this child," and the baby is subsequently born lifeless. Justify your answer.
questions.a: This is dramatic irony. The grandmother and the reader know the mother desperately wants the child, but neither knows the baby will be born stillborn — making the grandmother's worry about chloroform harming the baby tragically ironic because the baby arrives already "harmed" (lifeless). The character's limited knowledge contrasts with the unfolding reality. A wrong answer (e.g., calling it situational or verbal irony) indicates the student cannot differentiate irony types based on knowledge gaps between characters and audience.

questions.q: Compare the symbolic function of the "oil lamp" in the bedroom at the start of the delivery with the "dawn" that appears when the child is born. How do these two light-symbols mark a thematic shift?
questions.a: The oil lamp represents the dim, confined, anxious atmosphere of the old order — tradition, uncertainty, and the enclosed space of the mother's labour. The dawn symbolizes the arrival of new life, knowledge, and hope — a natural, expansive light that coincides with the child's first breath (and later, its revival). The shift from artificial, flickering lamp to broad daylight mirrors Andrew's internal shift from doubt to professional certainty. A weak answer treats both merely as setting details without connecting them to the story's thematic arc.

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: "The greatest irony in 'Birth' is not that the baby survives, but that Andrew — who entered the house viewing marriage as a 'dismal failure' — leaves having participated in the most profound affirmation of life and family." Defend or challenge with textual evidence.
questions.a: The statement is defensible. Andrew's internal monologue before the delivery dwells on failed marriages (Bramwell, Page, Denny) and his "level, doubting mind" conflicts with his "overflowing heart" for Christine. The night's work — saving a mother and child after twenty years of waiting — becomes a lived counter-argument to his cynicism. His final thought, "I've done something real at last," confirms the irony: the very institution he doubted (marriage/family) becomes the site of his redemption. A poor evaluation ignores Andrew's pre-delivery thoughts or treats the baby's survival as the sole irony.

questions.q: Write a 4-line poetic stanza that uses symbolism to capture the moment Andrew realizes the baby is breathing. Use at least two symbols from the story (e.g., the white fish, the iridescent bubble, the dawn, the rough towel).
questions.a: A strong stanza might read: "The white fish slips from death's cold hold, / An iridescent bubble breaks the grey / Dawn sweeps the floor where towels fold / Life wears the rough towel's fray." This uses the "white fish" (fragility), "iridescent bubble" (first breath), "dawn" (new beginning), and "rough towel" (human effort). A weak answer merely describes the scene without metaphorical compression or symbolic resonance.
